lessons.title: Show how you know
lessons.summary: Use a number line, a bar and pairs of counters to explain a short calculation.
lessons.objective: Use a number line, a bar and pairs of counters to explain a short calculation.
lessons.before: Mark the starting level first. For each lift move, find a new level on the line. Then compare the route with the distance between its ends.
lessons.ideas:
Going up adds to the current level. Going down subtracts. To count the total distance, add the lengths of all moves.

A fraction compares some equal parts with all the equal parts. Another complete batch keeps that fraction the same.

A pair adds two. When an odd number of singles is added, the complete display still has one item left after pairing.
lessons.method:
Show one calculation for the finishing level and another for the distance travelled.

Draw the whole bar and count the parts before calculating.

A reason about any number of pairs earns more than a list of separate examples.
mistakes: The last level can be negative even when the distance travelled is positive. These numbers answer different questions.
Using the number of yellow parts as the denominator would compare blue to yellow, rather than blue to the whole.
Several examples can suggest a rule. Explain what changing the number of pairs does to the spare item.

examples.title: A route between floors
examples.question:
A lift starts on level -5. It goes up 7 levels and then down 3 levels. Level 0 is the entrance.

  1. Which level does the lift reach?

    [2]

  2. How many levels does the lift travel in total?

    [2]

  3. Describe one move that returns the lift to its starting level.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) A move up adds 7. After that move the lift is on level 2.

A move down subtracts 3. \(2-3=-1\)

\(-1\)

(b) Both moves add to the distance travelled. Add the lengths 7 and 3.

\(10\)

(c) Compare the finishing level -1 with the starting level -5.

Go down 4 levels.

examples.title: Two colours, one batch
examples.question:
Each batch for a school event has 2 blue bands and 3 yellow bands. The organisers pack 20 bands using whole batches.

  1. How many bands are blue?

    [2]

  2. What fraction of the whole batch is blue? Give your answer in simplest form.

    [2]

  3. A volunteer packs 15 yellow bands. How many blue bands should go with them?

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Each batch has 5 bands. There are \(20\div 5=4\) batches.

There are 2 blue bands in each batch. Multiply by 4.

\(8\)

(b) Use 2 blue bands over 5 bands altogether, then simplify.

\(\frac{2}{5}\)

(c) Divide the yellow count by 3 to find the new number of batches. Each batch needs 2 blue bands.

\(10\)

examples.title: Pairs and spares
examples.question:
A display has 11 pairs of books and 3 single books on a shelf.

  1. How many books are in the display?

    [2]

  2. The number of pairs changes but the number of singles stays the same. Explain why the total is always odd.

    [2]

  3. Another display of this kind has 37 items. How many pairs are there?

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) There are two in each pair. Multiply 11 by 2, then add the 3 singles.

\(25\)

(b) Group all the items into twos. The singles also leave one unmatched object when put into twos.

Pairs make an even total. The fixed number of singles is odd, so the total is odd.

(c) Remove the 3 singles, then divide the rest by 2.

\(17\)

Each batch for a school event has 2 blue bands and 6 yellow bands. The organisers pack 80 bands using whole batches.

  1. How many bands are blue?

questions.prompt_html:
A display has 8 pairs of counters and 1 single counters on a shelf.

  1. How many counters are in the display?

    [2]

  2. The number of pairs changes but the number of singles stays the same. Explain why the total is always odd.

    [2]

  3. Another display of this kind has 29 items. How many pairs are there?

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(17\)

(b) Pairs make an even total. The fixed number of singles is odd, so the total is odd.

(c) \(14\)
questions.solution_html:
(a) There are two in each pair. Multiply 8 by 2, then add the 1 singles.

\(17\)

(b) Group all the items into twos. The singles also leave one unmatched object when put into twos.

Pairs make an even total. The fixed number of singles is odd, so the total is odd.

(c) Remove the 1 singles, then divide the rest by 2.

\(14\)
